arXiv:quant-ph/0601110v2 [quant-ph] 01 Feb 2006

On multipartite invariant states II.
Orthogonal symmetry.

Dariusz Chruściński and Andrzej Kossakowski ††thanks: email: darch@phys.uni.torun.pl Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Nicolaus Copernicus University,
Grudzia̧dzka 5/7, 87–100 Toruń, Poland
Abstract

We construct a new class of multipartite states possessing orthogonal symmetry. This new class defines a convex hull of multipartite states which are invariant under the action of local unitary operations introduced in our previous paper On multipartite invariant states I. Unitary symmetry. We study basic properties of multipartite symmetric states: separability criteria and multi-PPT conditions.

pacs
03.65.Ud, 03.67.-a

I Introduction

In a recent paper [1] we analyzed multipartite states invariant under local unitary operations. For bipartite systems one has two classes of unitary invariant states: Werner states [2] invariant under

ρ⟶U⊗U​ρ​(U⊗U)†,\rho\ \longrightarrow\ U{\,\otimes\,}U\,\rho\,(U{\,\otimes\,}U)^{\dagger}\ , (1)

for any U∈U⁡(d)U\in U(d), where U⁡(d)U(d) denotes the group of unitary d×dd\times d matrices, and isotropic states [3] which are invariant under

ρ⟶U⊗U¯​ρ​(U⊗U¯)†,\rho\ \longrightarrow\ U{\,\otimes\,}\overline{U}\,\rho\,(U{\,\otimes\,}\overline{U})^{\dagger}\ , (2)

where U¯\overline{U} is the complex conjugate of UU in some basis. In [1] we proposed a natural generalization of bipartite symmetric states to multipartite systems consisting of an arbitrary even number of dd-dimensional subsystems (qudits).

In the present paper we introduce a new class of states which combines above symmetries (1) and (2), i.e. it contains states which are both U⊗UU{\,\otimes\,}U and U⊗U¯U{\,\otimes\,}\overline{U}–invariant, that is, states invariant under all unitary operations UU such that U=U¯U=\overline{U}:

ρ⟶O⊗O​ρ​(O⊗O)T,\rho\ \longrightarrow\ O{\,\otimes\,}O\,\rho\,(O{\,\otimes\,}O)^{T}\ , (3)

with O∈O⁡(d)⊂U⁡(d)O\in O(d)\subset U(d), where O⁡(d)O(d) denotes the set of d×dd\times d orthogonal matrices. Such states were first considered in [4] (see also [5]). In a slightly different context symmetric states were studied also in [6]. Recently [7] unitary invariant 3-partite states were used to test multipartite separability criteria.

Here we present a general construction of O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant states for multipartite systems consisting of an arbitrary even number of dd-dimensional subsystems. It turns out that orthogonally invariant states of 2​K2K–partite system (with KK being a positive integer) define (3K−1)(3^{K}-1)–invariant simplex. We analyze (multi)separability criteria and the hierarchy of multi-PPT conditions [1, 8, 9]. It is hoped that these new family would serve as a useful laboratory to study multipartite entanglement [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15].

II Bipartite states

II.1 Simplex of orthogonally invariant states

Let us consider a bipartite Alice–Bob system living in ℋA​B=ℋA⊗ℋB=(ℂd)⊗ 2\mathcal{H}_{AB}=\mathcal{H}_{A}{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{B}=(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{{\,\otimes\,}2}. Recall that the space of U⊗UU{\,\otimes\,}U–invariant hermitian operators in ℋA​B\mathcal{H}_{AB} is spanned by two orthogonal projectors

Q0=12​(I⊗ 2+𝐅),Q1=12​(I⊗ 2−𝐅),Q^{0}=\frac{1}{2}(I^{{\,\otimes\,}2}+\mathbf{F})\ ,\ \ \ Q^{1}=\frac{1}{2}(I^{{\,\otimes\,}2}-\mathbf{F})\ , (4)

where 𝐅{\bf F} is a flip operator, i.e. 𝐅⁡(ψ⊗φ)=φ⊗ψ\mathbf{F}(\psi{\,\otimes\,}\varphi)=\varphi{\,\otimes\,}\psi, defined by

𝐅=∑i,j=1d|i​j⟩​⟨j​i|.\mathbf{F}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}\,|ij\rangle\langle ji|\ . (5)

In particular this 2-dimensional space contains a line of normalized (i.e. with unit trace) operators:

L:(1−q)Q~0+qQ~1,L:\ \ \ (1-q)\,\widetilde{Q}^{0}+q\,\widetilde{Q}^{1}\ , (6)

with q∈ℝq\in\mathbb{R}, and throughout the paper A~\widetilde{A} stands for A/Tr​AA/\mbox{Tr}A. A segment of LL with vertices Q~0\widetilde{Q}^{0} and Q~1\widetilde{Q}^{1} defines a family of bipartite Werner states:

𝒲𝐪=q0​Q~0+q1​Q~1,\mathcal{W}_{\bf q}=q_{0}\,\widetilde{Q}^{0}+q_{1}\,\widetilde{Q}^{1}\ , (7)

with qα≥0q_{\alpha}\geq 0, and q0+q1=1q_{0}+q_{1}=1.

Now, a partial transposition 1​l⊗τ{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau sends points of LL into another line Lτ=(1​l⊗τ)​LL_{\tau}=({\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau)L:

Lτ:(1−p)P~0+pP~1,L_{\tau}:\ \ \ (1-p)\,\widetilde{P}^{0}+p\,\widetilde{P}^{1}\ , (8)

with p∈ℝp\in\mathbb{R}, and PαP^{\alpha} denote the following orthogonal projectors:

P1=Pd+,P0=I⊗ 2−P1,P^{1}=P^{+}_{d}\ ,\ \ \ P^{0}=I^{{\,\otimes\,}2}-P^{1}\ , (9)

with Pd+P^{+}_{d} being a 1-dimensional projector corresponding to a canonical maximally entangled state in ℂd⊗ℂd{\mathbb{C}^{d}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathbb{C}^{d}}:

Pd+=1d​(1​l⊗τ)​𝐅=1d​∑i,j=1d|i​i⟩​⟨j​j|.P^{+}_{d}=\frac{1}{d}\,({\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau){\bf F}=\frac{1}{d}\,\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}\,|ii\rangle\langle jj|\ . (10)

A segment of LτL_{\tau} with vertices P~0\widetilde{P}^{0} and P~1\widetilde{P}^{1} defines a family of bipartite isotropic states:

ℐ𝐩=p0​P~0+p1​P~1,\mathcal{I}_{\bf p}=p_{0}\,\widetilde{P}^{0}+p_{1}\,\widetilde{P}^{1}\ , (11)

with pα≥0p_{\alpha}\geq 0, and p0+p1=1p_{0}+p_{1}=1.

Let us introduce a new class Σ1\Sigma_{1} of bipartite states which are both U⊗UU{\,\otimes\,}U and U⊗U¯U{\,\otimes\,}\overline{U}–invariant for all U∈U⁡(d)U\in U(d) such that U=U¯U=\overline{U}. Such UU’s represent real orthogonal matrices in O⁡(d)O(d). Hence, Σ1\Sigma_{1} defines a new family of symmetric O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant states:

ρ⟶O⊗O​ρ​(O⊗O)T,\rho\ \longrightarrow\ O{\,\otimes\,}O\,\rho\,(O{\,\otimes\,}O)^{T}\ , (12)

with O∈O⁡(d)⊂U⁡(d)O\in O(d)\subset U(d). Clearly Σ1\Sigma_{1} contains both Werner and isotropic states and, therefore, it contains a convex hull of Q~α\widetilde{Q}^{\alpha} and P~α\widetilde{P}^{\alpha}:

Σ1⊃conv​{Q~0,Q~1,P~0,P~1}.\Sigma_{1}\supset\mbox{conv}\,\{\widetilde{Q}^{0},\widetilde{Q}^{1},\widetilde{P}^{0},\widetilde{P}^{1}\}\ . (13)

It is easy to see that these four states are co-planar, i.e. they belong to a common 2-dimensional plane in d2d^{2}-dimensional space of hermitian operators in ℂd⊗ℂd{\mathbb{C}^{d}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathbb{C}^{d}}. Indeed, one shows that

det​[Tr​(Q~α​Q~β)Tr​(Q~α​P~β)Tr​(P~α​Q~β)Tr​(P~α​P~β)]=0,\mbox{det}\left[\begin{array}[]{c|c}\mbox{Tr}(\widetilde{Q}^{\alpha}\widetilde{Q}^{\beta})&\mbox{Tr}(\widetilde{Q}^{\alpha}\widetilde{P}^{\beta})\\ \hline\cr\mbox{Tr}(\widetilde{P}^{\alpha}\widetilde{Q}^{\beta})&\mbox{Tr}(\widetilde{P}^{\alpha}\widetilde{P}^{\beta})\end{array}\right]=0\ , (14)

and hence Σ1\Sigma_{1} is 2-dimensional. Therefore the two lines LL and LτL_{\tau} intersect and the point L∩LτL\cap L_{\tau} is described by

q=12−1d⁡(d+1),q=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{d(d+1)}\ , (15)

and

p=2d⁡(d+1)​[12+1d⁡(d+1)].p=\frac{2}{d(d+1)}\left[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{d(d+1)}\right]\ . (16)

Note that q,p∈[0,1]q,p\in[0,1] and hence the intersection point L∩Lτ∈Σ1L\cap L_{\tau}\in\Sigma_{1} defines a state which is both Werner and isotropic. Moreover, since q<1/2q<1/2 (and p<1/dp<1/d) this state is separable.

Now, it turns out that Σ1\Sigma_{1} defines a simplex with vertices Π~α;α=0,1,2\widetilde{\Pi}^{\alpha};\ \alpha=0,1,2, where

Π0\displaystyle\Pi^{0} =\displaystyle= Q0−P1,\displaystyle Q^{0}-P^{1}\ ,
Π1\displaystyle\Pi^{1} =\displaystyle= Q1,\displaystyle Q^{1}\ , (17)
Π2\displaystyle\Pi^{2} =\displaystyle= P1.\displaystyle P^{1}\ .

One may call it a ’minimal simplex’ containing conv​{Q~0,Q~1,P~0,P~1}\mbox{conv}\,\{\widetilde{Q}^{0},\widetilde{Q}^{1},\widetilde{P}^{0},\widetilde{P}^{1}\}. In particular

Q~0=1d⁡(d+1)​[(d−1)​(d+2)​Π~0+2​Π~2],\widetilde{Q}^{0}=\frac{1}{d(d+1)}\,\left[(d-1)(d+2)\,\widetilde{\Pi}^{0}+2\widetilde{\Pi}^{2}\right]\ , (18)

and

P~0=12​(d+1)​[(d+2)​Π~0+d​Π~1].\widetilde{P}^{0}=\frac{1}{2(d+1)}\,\left[(d+2)\,\widetilde{\Pi}^{0}+d\widetilde{\Pi}^{1}\right]\ . (19)

Note, that the family Πk\Pi^{k} gives rise to the orthogonal resolution of identity in ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}_{A}{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{B}:

Πi​Πj=δi​j​Πj,\Pi^{i}\Pi^{j}=\delta_{ij}\Pi^{j}\ , (20)

and

Π0+Π1+Π2=I⊗ 2.\Pi^{0}+\Pi^{1}+\Pi^{2}=I^{{\,\otimes\,}2}\ . (21)

Any state ρ\rho in Σ1\Sigma_{1} may be written as follows

ρ=∑k=02πk​Π~k,\rho=\sum_{k=0}^{2}\,\pi_{k}\,\widetilde{\Pi}^{k}\ , (22)

where Π~k=Πk/Tr​Πk\widetilde{\Pi}^{k}=\Pi^{k}/\mbox{Tr}\Pi^{k}, and the corresponding ‘fidelities’

πk=Tr​(ρ​Πk),\pi_{k}=\mbox{Tr}(\rho\Pi^{k})\ , (23)

satisfy πk≥0\pi_{k}\geq 0 together with ∑kπk=1\sum_{k}\pi_{k}=1. It is evident that an arbitrary bipartite state ρ\rho may be projected onto the O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant subspace by the following projection operation 𝐏(1):𝒫⟶Σ1\,\mathbf{P}^{(1)}:\mathcal{P}\longrightarrow\Sigma_{1}:

𝐏(1)​ρ=∑k=02Tr​(ρ​𝚷k)​Π~k.\mathbf{P}^{(1)}\rho=\sum_{k=0}^{2}\,\mbox{Tr}(\rho\mathbf{\Pi}^{k})\,\widetilde{\Pi}^{k}\ . (24)

II.2 Separability and PPT condition

Consider a separable state σ=Pψ⊗Pφ\sigma=P_{\psi}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi}, where Px=|x⟩​⟨x|P_{x}=|x\rangle\langle x|, and ψ,φ\psi,\varphi are normalized vectors in ℂd{\mathbb{C}^{d}}. One easily finds for fidelities Tr​(σ​Πk)\mbox{Tr}(\sigma\Pi^{k}):

π0\displaystyle\pi_{0} =\displaystyle= 12​(1+α)−βd,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(1+\alpha)-\frac{\beta}{d}\ ,
π1\displaystyle\pi_{1} =\displaystyle= 12​(1−α),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(1-\alpha)\ , (25)
π2\displaystyle\pi_{2} =\displaystyle= βd,\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{d}\ ,

where

α=|⟨ψ|φ⟩|2,β=|⟨ψ|φ¯⟩|2.\alpha=|\langle\psi|\varphi\rangle|^{2}\ ,\ \ \ \ \beta=|\langle\psi|\overline{\varphi}\rangle|^{2}\ . (26)

Now, an arbitrary separable state is a convex combination of the extremal product states Pψ⊗PφP_{\psi}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi}. Noting that 0≤α,β≤10\leq\alpha,\beta\leq 1, the separable O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant states satisfy

π1≤12,π2≤1d,\pi_{1}\leq\frac{1}{2}\ ,\ \ \ \ \pi_{2}\leq\frac{1}{d}\ , (27)

i.e. they combine separability conditions for Werner states π1≤1/2\pi_{1}\leq 1/2 and isotropic states π2≤1/d\pi_{2}\leq 1/d.

Now, applying a partial transposition (1​l⊗τ)({\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau) to (22) one finds

(1​l⊗τ)​ρ=∑α=02πα′​Π~k,({\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau)\rho=\sum_{\alpha=0}^{2}\,\pi^{\prime}_{\alpha}\,\widetilde{\Pi}^{k}\ , (28)

where

πα′=∑β=02πβ​𝐂β​α,\pi^{\prime}_{\alpha}=\sum_{\beta=0}^{2}\,\pi_{\beta}\,\mathbf{C}^{\beta\alpha}\ , (29)

and 𝐂\mathbf{C} denotes the following 3×33\times 3 matrix:

𝐂=12​d​(d−2d2d+2d−2(d−1)​(d+2)−d⁡(d−1)2).\mathbf{C}=\frac{1}{2d}\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccr}d-2&d&2\\ d+2&d&-2\\ (d-1)(d+2)&-d(d-1)&2\end{array}\right)\ . (30)

Observe that

∑β=02𝐂β​α=1,\sum_{\beta=0}^{2}\,\mathbf{C}^{\beta\alpha}=1\ , (31)

but 𝐂β​α\mathbf{C}^{\beta\alpha} contains negative elements and hence it is not a stochastic matrix. The Peres-Horodecki condition [8, 9] implies πα′≥0\pi^{\prime}_{\alpha}\geq 0 and hence

π0+π1−(d−1)​π2\displaystyle\pi_{0}+\pi_{1}-(d-1)\pi_{2} ≥\displaystyle\geq 0,\displaystyle 0\ , (32)
π0−π1+π2\displaystyle\pi_{0}-\pi_{1}+\pi_{2} ≥\displaystyle\geq 0,\displaystyle 0\ , (33)

which is equivalent to π1≤1/2\pi_{1}\leq 1/2 and π2≤1/d\pi_{2}\leq 1/d. This shows that bipartite O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant state is separable iff it is PPT.

III 2×22\times 2–partite states

III.1 Construction

Consider now a 4-partite system living in ℋ1⊗ℋ2⊗ℋ3⊗ℋ4\mathcal{H}_{1}{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{2}{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{3}{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{4} with ℋk=ℂd\mathcal{H}_{k}={\mathbb{C}^{d}}. Following [1] we may introduce two Alices AkA_{k} and two Bobs BkB_{k}: AkA_{k} lives in ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} and BkB_{k} lives in ℋ2+k\mathcal{H}_{2+k} (for k=1,2k=1,2).

Let 𝜶\alpha be a trinary 22-dimensional vector, i.e. 𝝈=(α1,α2)\mbox{\boldmath$\sigma$}=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}) with αj∈{0,1,2}\alpha_{j}\in\{0,1,2\}. Following [1] we define a family of 44–partite projectors

𝚷𝜶=Π1|3α1⊗Π2|4α2,\mathbf{\Pi}^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}=\Pi^{\alpha_{1}}_{1|3}{\,\otimes\,}\Pi^{\alpha_{2}}_{2|4}\ , (34)

where Li|jL_{i|j} denotes a bipartite operator acting on ℋi⊗ℋj\mathcal{H}_{i}{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{j}, and Πα\Pi^{\alpha} are defined in (17). One easily shows that 9 projectors (34) satisfy

  1. 1.

    𝚷𝜶\ \ \mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}} are 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant, i.e.

    𝐎⊗𝐎​𝚷𝜶=𝚷𝜶​𝐎⊗𝐎,\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}\,\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}=\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}\ , (35)

    with 𝐎=(O1,O2)\mathbf{O}=(O_{1},O_{2}), and

    𝐎⊗𝐎=O1⊗O2⊗O1⊗O2.\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}=O_{1}{\,\otimes\,}O_{2}{\,\otimes\,}O_{1}{\,\otimes\,}O_{2}\ .
  2. 2.

    𝚷𝜶⋅𝚷𝜷=δ𝜶𝜷​𝚷𝜷\ \ \mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}=\delta_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}}\,\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}},

  3. 3.

    ∑𝜶𝚷𝜶= 1​l⊗ 4,\ \ \sum_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\,\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,=\,{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}^{{\,\otimes\,}4}\ ,

that is, 𝚷𝜶\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}} define spectral resolution of identity in (ℂd)⊗ 4(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{{\,\otimes\,}4}. Hence, any 4-partite 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant state may be uniquely represented by

ρ=∑𝜶π𝜶​𝚷~𝜶,\rho=\sum_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\ , (36)

where the corresponding ‘fidelities’ π𝜶=Tr​(ρ​𝚷𝜶)\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}=\mbox{Tr}(\rho\,{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}) satisfy π𝜶≥0\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\geq 0 together with ∑𝜶π𝜶=1\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}=1. The above construction gives rise to 8-dimensional simplex Σ2\Sigma_{2} with vertices 𝚷~𝜶\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}. Note, that Σ2\Sigma_{2} contains a convex hull of 4 classes of 4-partite invariant states introduced in [1]:

Σ2⊃conv​{Σ2(00),Σ2(01),Σ2(10),Σ2(11)},\Sigma_{2}\supset\mbox{conv}\,\Big\{\Sigma^{(00)}_{2},\Sigma^{(01)}_{2},\Sigma^{(10)}_{2},\Sigma^{(11)}_{2}\Big\}\ , (37)

where

Σ2(00)\displaystyle\Sigma^{(00)}_{2} =\displaystyle= conv​{Q~1|3i⊗Q~2|4j},\displaystyle\mbox{conv}\,\{\widetilde{Q}^{i}_{1|3}{\,\otimes\,}\widetilde{Q}^{j}_{2|4}\}\ , (38)
Σ2(01)\displaystyle\Sigma^{(01)}_{2} =\displaystyle= conv​{Q~1|3i⊗P~2|4j},\displaystyle\mbox{conv}\,\{\widetilde{Q}^{i}_{1|3}{\,\otimes\,}\widetilde{P}^{j}_{2|4}\}\ , (39)
Σ2(10)\displaystyle\Sigma^{(10)}_{2} =\displaystyle= conv​{P~1|3i⊗Q~2|4j},\displaystyle\mbox{conv}\,\{\widetilde{P}^{i}_{1|3}{\,\otimes\,}\widetilde{Q}^{j}_{2|4}\}\ , (40)
Σ2(11)\displaystyle\Sigma^{(11)}_{2} =\displaystyle= conv​{P~1|3i⊗P~2|4j},\displaystyle\mbox{conv}\,\{\widetilde{P}^{i}_{1|3}{\,\otimes\,}\widetilde{P}^{j}_{2|4}\}\ , (41)

with i,j∈{0,1}i,j\in\{0,1\}. A 3-dimensional simplex Σ2𝒂\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{2}, where  𝒂=(a1,a2){\mbox{ \boldmath$a$}}=(a_{1},a_{2}) denotes 2-dimensional binary vector, defines a set of 𝒂a-invariant states. Recall that a 4-partite state ρ\rho is 𝒂a–invariant iff τ𝒂​ρ\tau_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}\rho, with

τ𝒂=1​l⊗ 1​l⊗τa1⊗τa2,\tau_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau^{a_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau^{a_{2}}\ , (42)

is 𝐔⊗𝐔\mathbf{U}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{U}–invariant. In particular Σ2(00)\Sigma^{(00)}_{2} and Σ2(11)\Sigma^{(11)}_{2} denote 4-partite Werner and isotropic states, respectively.

III.2 Separability

To find the corresponding separability criteria note that a general 4-partite O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant state ρ\rho is 4-separable iff there exists a 4-separable state σ\sigma such that 𝐏(2)​ρ=σ\mathbf{P}^{(2)}\rho=\sigma, where

𝐏(2):𝒫⟶Σ2,\mathbf{P}^{(2)}:\mathcal{P}\longrightarrow\Sigma_{2}\ , (43)

defines a projection onto 4-partite O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant states. Consider an extremal product state σ=Pψ1⊗Pψ2⊗Pφ1⊗Pφ2\sigma=P_{\psi_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\psi_{2}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{2}}, where ψi,φj\psi_{i},\varphi_{j} are normalized vectors in ℂd{\mathbb{C}^{d}}. One easily finds for fidelities Tr​(σ​Π𝝈)\mbox{Tr}(\sigma\Pi^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\sigma$}}):

π𝝈\displaystyle\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\sigma$}} =\displaystyle= Tr​(Pψ1⊗Pφ1⋅Π1|3σ1)​Tr​(Pψ2⊗Pφ2⋅Π2|4σ2)\displaystyle\mbox{Tr}(P_{\psi_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{1}}\cdot\Pi_{1|3}^{\sigma_{1}})\,\mbox{Tr}(P_{\psi_{2}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{2}}\cdot\Pi_{2|4}^{\sigma_{2}}) (44)
=\displaystyle= u1⋅u2,\displaystyle u_{1}\cdot u_{2}\ ,

with

ui={(1+αi)/2−βi/d,σi=0(1−αi)/2,σi=1βi/d,σi=2,u_{i}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(1+\alpha_{i})/2-\beta_{i}/d&\ ,\ \ \sigma_{i}=0\\ (1-\alpha_{i})/2&\ ,\ \ \sigma_{i}=1\\ \beta_{i}/d&\ ,\ \ \sigma_{i}=2\end{array}\right.\ , (45)

where

αi=|⟨ψi|φi⟩|2,βi=|⟨ψi|φ¯i⟩|2.\alpha_{i}=|\langle\psi_{i}|\varphi_{i}\rangle|^{2}\ ,\ \ \ \ \beta_{i}=|\langle\psi_{i}|\overline{\varphi}_{i}\rangle|^{2}\ . (46)

Now, since αi,βi≤1\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\leq 1, the projection 𝐏(2)\mathbf{P}^{(2)} of the convex hull of extremal separable states gives the subset of separable O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant states defined by the following relations:

π𝝈≤1fσ1​fσ2,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\sigma$}}\leq\frac{1}{f_{\sigma_{1}}f_{\sigma_{2}}}\ , (47)

where

fσ={1,σ=02,σ=1d,σ=2.f_{\sigma}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&,\ \sigma=0\\ 2&,\ \sigma=1\\ d&,\ \sigma=2\end{array}\right.\ . (48)

It is evident, that (47) generalize formulae (27). Clearly, separable states in Σ2\Sigma_{2} contain a convex hull of separable states in each 𝒂a–invariant simplex Σ2𝒂\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{2}:

Sep​(Σ2)⊃conv​⋃𝒂Sep​(Σ2𝒂).\mbox{Sep}(\Sigma_{2})\supset\mbox{conv}\,\bigcup_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}}\,\mbox{Sep}(\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{2})\ . (49)

Is 4-separability equivalent to PPT condition? Note, that one may perform 3 different partial transpositions (42):

τ(01)\displaystyle\tau_{(01)} =\displaystyle= 1​l⊗ 1​l⊗ 1​l⊗τ,\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau\ ,
τ(10)\displaystyle\tau_{(10)} =\displaystyle= 1​l⊗ 1​l⊗τ⊗ 1​l,\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau{\,\otimes\,}{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}\ , (50)
τ(11)\displaystyle\tau_{(11)} =\displaystyle= 1​l⊗ 1​l⊗τ⊗τ.\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}{\,\otimes\,}\tau{\,\otimes\,}\tau\ .

It is easy to see that

τ(01)​ρ\displaystyle\tau_{(01)}\,\rho =\displaystyle= ∑𝜶π𝜶′​𝚷~𝜶,\displaystyle\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\pi^{\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\ , (51)
τ(10)​ρ\displaystyle\tau_{(10)}\,\rho =\displaystyle= ∑𝜶π𝜶′′​𝚷~𝜶,\displaystyle\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\pi^{\prime\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\ , (52)
τ(11)​ρ\displaystyle\tau_{(11)}\,\rho =\displaystyle= ∑𝜶π𝜶′′′​𝚷~𝜶,\displaystyle\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\pi^{\prime\prime\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\ , (53)

with

π𝜶′\displaystyle\pi^{\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}} =\displaystyle= ∑𝜷π𝜷​(𝐈⊗𝐂)𝜷𝜶,\displaystyle\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,(\mathbf{I}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{C})^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\ , (54)
π𝜶′′\displaystyle\pi^{\prime\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}} =\displaystyle= ∑𝜷π𝜷​(𝐂⊗𝐈)𝜷𝜶,\displaystyle\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,(\mathbf{C}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{I})^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\ , (55)
π𝜶′′′\displaystyle\pi^{\prime\prime\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}} =\displaystyle= ∑𝜷π𝜷​(𝐂⊗𝐂)𝜷𝜶,\displaystyle\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,(\mathbf{C}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{C})^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\ , (56)

where 𝐈\mathbf{I} denotes 3×33\times 3 identity matrix and 𝐂\mathbf{C} is defined in (30). For example one finds that a state ρ∈Σ2\rho\in\Sigma_{2} is (01)(01)–PPT, i.e. τ01​ρ≥0\tau_{01}\rho\geq 0 iff

π00+π01−(d−1)​π02\displaystyle\pi_{00}+\pi_{01}-(d-1)\pi_{02} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π00−π01+π02\displaystyle\pi_{00}-\pi_{01}+\pi_{02} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π10+π11−(d−1)​π12\displaystyle\pi_{10}+\pi_{11}-(d-1)\pi_{12} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ , (57)
π10−π11+π12\displaystyle\pi_{10}-\pi_{11}+\pi_{12} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π20+π21−(d−1)​π22\displaystyle\pi_{20}+\pi_{21}-(d-1)\pi_{22} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π20−π21+π22\displaystyle\pi_{20}-\pi_{21}+\pi_{22} ≥0.\displaystyle\geq 0\ .

Similarly, it is (10)(10)–PPT iff

π00+π10−(d−1)​π20\displaystyle\pi_{00}+\pi_{10}-(d-1)\pi_{20} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π00−π10+π20\displaystyle\pi_{00}-\pi_{10}+\pi_{20} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π01+π11−(d−1)​π21\displaystyle\pi_{01}+\pi_{11}-(d-1)\pi_{21} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ , (58)
π01−π11+π21\displaystyle\pi_{01}-\pi_{11}+\pi_{21} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π02+π12−(d−1)​π22\displaystyle\pi_{02}+\pi_{12}-(d-1)\pi_{22} ≥0,\displaystyle\geq 0\ ,
π02−π12+π22\displaystyle\pi_{02}-\pi_{12}+\pi_{22} ≥0.\displaystyle\geq 0\ .

Now, it was proved in [1] that any 4-partite 𝐔⊗𝐔\mathbf{U}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{U}–invariant state is 4-separable iff it is (01)(01)- (10)(10)- and (11)(11)-PPT. Moreover, any symmetric state is A|BA|B bi-separable iff it is (11)(11)–PPT. We conjecture that the same property holds for 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant states. To prove it one has to apply the same techniques as in [1]. To investigate all PPT conditions one needs together with (57) and (58) a highly complicated (11)(11)–PPT condition which we shall not consider here.

IV 2​K2K–partite states

IV.1 General contruction

Generalization to 2​K2K–partite system is straightforward. Following [1] we introduce 2​K2K qudits with the total space ℋ=ℋ1⊗…⊗ℋ2​K=(ℂd)⊗ 2​K\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{2K}=(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{{\,\otimes\,}2K}. We may still interpret the total system as a bipartite one with ℋA=ℋ1⊗…⊗ℋK\mathcal{H}_{A}=\mathcal{H}_{1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{K} and ℋB=ℋK+1⊗…⊗ℋ2​K\mathcal{H}_{B}=\mathcal{H}_{K+1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{2K}. Equivalently, we may introduce KK Alices and KK Bobs with ℋAi=ℋi\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}}=\mathcal{H}_{i} and ℋBi=ℋK+i\mathcal{H}_{B_{i}}=\mathcal{H}_{K+i}, respectively. Then ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A} and ℋB\mathcal{H}_{B} stand for the composite KK Alices’ and Bobs’ spaces.

Now, let 𝜶\alpha be a trinary KK-dimensional vector, i.e. 𝝈=(α1,…,αK)\mbox{\boldmath$\sigma$}=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{K}) with αj∈{0,1,2}\alpha_{j}\in\{0,1,2\}. In analogy to (34) let us define a family of 2​K2K–partite projectors

𝚷𝜶=Π1|K+1α1⊗…⊗ΠK|2​KαK.\mathbf{\Pi}^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}=\Pi^{\alpha_{1}}_{1|K+1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\Pi^{\alpha_{K}}_{K|2K}\ . (59)

One easily shows that

  1. 1.

    𝚷𝜶\ \ \mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}} are 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant, i.e.

    𝐎⊗𝐎​𝚷𝜶=𝚷𝜶​𝐎⊗𝐎,\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}\,\mathbf{\Pi}^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}=\mathbf{\Pi}^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}\ , (60)

    with 𝐎=(O1,…,OK)\mathbf{O}=(O_{1},\ldots,O_{K}), and

    𝐎⊗𝐎=O1⊗…⊗OK⊗O1⊗…⊗OK.\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}=O_{1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}O_{K}{\,\otimes\,}O_{1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}O_{K}\ .
  2. 2.

    𝚷𝜶⋅𝚷𝜷=δ𝜶𝜷​𝚷𝜷\ \ \mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\cdot\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}=\delta_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}}\,\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}},

  3. 3.

    ∑𝜶𝚷𝜶= 1​l⊗ 2​K.\ \ \sum_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\,\mathbf{\Pi}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,=\,{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}^{{\,\otimes\,}2K}\ .

Therefore, 2​K2K–partite 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant states define a (3K−1)(3^{K}-1)–dimensional simplex ΣK\Sigma_{K}:

ρ=∑𝜶π𝜶​𝚷~𝜶,\rho=\sum_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\ , (61)

where

𝚷~𝜶=Π~1|K+1α1⊗…⊗Π~K|2​KαK,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}=\widetilde{\Pi}^{\alpha_{1}}_{1|K+1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\widetilde{\Pi}^{\alpha_{K}}_{K|2K}\ , (62)

and the corresponding ‘fidelities’

π𝜶=Tr​(ρ​Π𝜶),\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}=\mbox{Tr}(\rho\Pi^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}})\ , (63)

satisfy π𝜶≥0\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\geq 0 together with ∑𝜶π𝜶=1\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}=1.

Denote by ΣK𝒂\Sigma_{K}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}} a (2K−1)(2^{K}-1)–dimensional simplex of 𝒂a–invariant states, where  𝒂=(a1,…,aK){\mbox{ \boldmath$a$}}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K}) denotes a binary KK-vector. Recall that a 2​K2K-partite state ρ\rho is 𝒂a–invariant iff τ𝒂​ρ\tau_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}\rho, with

τ𝒂=1​l⊗K⊗τa1⊗…⊗τaK,\tau_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}^{{\,\otimes\,}K}{\,\otimes\,}\tau^{a_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\tau^{a_{K}}\ , (64)

is 𝐔⊗𝐔\mathbf{U}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{U}–invariant. In particular ΣK(0​…​0)\Sigma^{(0\ldots 0)}_{K} and ΣK(1​…​1)\Sigma^{(1\ldots 1)}_{K} denote the simplex of 2​K2K-partite Werner and isotropic states, respectively (see [1]). It is therefore clear that ΣK\Sigma_{K} contains a convex hull of 2K2^{K} single 𝒂a-invariant simplexes ΣK𝒂\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{K}:

ΣK⊃conv​⋃𝒂ΣK𝒂.\Sigma_{K}\supset\mbox{conv}\,\bigcup_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}}\,\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{K}\ . (65)

IV.2 Separability and multi–PPT conditions

To find separability conditions for 2​K2K-partite 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant states consider a separable state

σ=Pψ1⊗…⊗PψK⊗Pφ1⊗…⊗PφK,\sigma=P_{\psi_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}P_{\psi_{K}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{K}}\ ,

where ψi,φj\psi_{i},\varphi_{j} are normalized vectors in ℂd{\mathbb{C}^{d}}. One easily finds for fidelities Tr​(σ​Π𝝈)\mbox{Tr}(\sigma\Pi^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\sigma$}}):

π𝝈\displaystyle\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\sigma$}} =\displaystyle= ∏i=1KTr​(Pψi⊗Pφi⋅Πi|K+iσi)\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{K}\,\mbox{Tr}(P_{\psi_{i}}{\,\otimes\,}P_{\varphi_{i}}\cdot\Pi_{i|K+i}^{\sigma_{i}}) (66)
=\displaystyle= u1​…​uK,\displaystyle u_{1}\,\ldots\,u_{K}\ ,

where uiu_{i} are defined in (45). The projection 𝐏(K)\mathbf{P}^{(K)} of the convex hull of extremal separable states gives the subset of separable O⊗OO{\,\otimes\,}O–invariant states defined by the following relations:

π𝝈≤1fσ1​…​fσK,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\sigma$}}\leq\frac{1}{f_{\sigma_{1}}\ldots f_{\sigma_{K}}}\ , (67)

where ff’s are defined in (48). Clearly, a set of separable states in ΣK\Sigma_{K} contains a convex hull of separable states in each 𝒂a–invariant simplex ΣK𝒂\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{K}:

Sep​(ΣK)⊃conv​⋃𝒂Sep​(ΣK𝒂).\mbox{Sep}(\Sigma_{K})\supset\mbox{conv}\,\bigcup_{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}}\,\mbox{Sep}(\Sigma^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}_{K})\ . (68)

For 2​K2K–partite state one may look for 2K−12^{K}-1 partial transpositions

τ𝒂=1​l⊗K⊗τa1⊗…⊗τaK.\tau_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}^{{\,\otimes\,}K}{\,\otimes\,}\tau^{a_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\tau^{a_{K}}\ . (69)

Note, that

τ𝒂​ρ=∑𝜶π𝜶′​𝚷~𝜶,\tau_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$a$}}\rho=\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\pi^{\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\,\widetilde{\mathbf{\Pi}}^{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}\ , (70)

with

π𝜶′=∑𝜷π𝜷​(𝐂a1⊗…⊗𝐂aK)𝜷𝜶,\pi^{\prime}_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}=\sum_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,\pi_{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}\,(\mathbf{C}^{a_{1}}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{C}^{a_{K}})^{{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\beta$}}{\mbox{\scriptsize\boldmath$\alpha$}}}\ , (71)

where

𝐂a={𝐈,a=0𝐂,a=1.{\bf C}^{a}\ =\ \left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\mathbf{I}&\ ,\ \ a=0\\ \mathbf{C}&\ ,\ \ a=1\end{array}\right.\ . (72)

In analogy to 4-partite symmetric states we conjecture that a 2​K2K-partite state in ΣK\Sigma_{K} is 2​K2K-separable iff it is 𝒃b-PPT for all binary 2-vectors 𝒃b. Moreover, a state in ΣK\Sigma_{K} is A|BA|B bi-separable iff it is (1​…​1)(1\ldots 1)–PPT.

IV.3 Reductions

It is evident that reducing the 2​K2K partite state ρ∈ΣK\rho\in\Sigma_{K} with respect to Ai⊗BiA_{i}{\,\otimes\,}B_{i} pair one obtains 2​(K−1)2(K-1)–partite state ρ′∈ΣK−1\rho^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{K-1} living in

ℋ1⊗…​ℋˇi⊗…⊗ℋˇi+K⊗…⊗ℋ2​K,\mathcal{H}_{1}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots\check{\mathcal{H}}_{i}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\check{\mathcal{H}}_{i+K}{\,\otimes\,}\ldots{\,\otimes\,}\mathcal{H}_{2K}\ , (73)

where ℋˇi\check{\mathcal{H}}_{i} denotes the omitting of ℋi{\mathcal{H}}_{i}. The corresponding fidelities are given by

π(α1​…​αK−1)′=∑βπ(α1​…​αi−1​β​αi​…​αK−1).\pi^{\prime}_{(\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{K-1})}\ =\ \sum_{\beta}\,\pi_{(\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{i-1}\beta\alpha_{i}\ldots\alpha_{K-1})}\ . (74)

Note, that reduction with respect to a ‘mixed’ pair, say Ai⊗BjA_{i}{\,\otimes\,}B_{j} with i≠ji\neq j, is equivalent to two ‘natural’ reductions with respect to Ai⊗BiA_{i}{\,\otimes\,}B_{i} and Aj⊗BjA_{j}{\,\otimes\,}B_{j} and hence it gives rise to 2​(K−2)2(K-2)–partite invariant state. This procedure establishes a natural hierarchy of multipartite 𝐎⊗𝐎\mathbf{O}{\,\otimes\,}\mathbf{O}–invariant states.
